No Silver Dollar

Game Strategy

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: you and the computer take turns sliding the same counters to the left. Whoever makes the last move wins.
How to play: pick a counter, then pick an empty square to its left. A counter cannot jump over another counter or share its square.

Slide the board sideways to see all of it.

Look for the math

The gaps between the counters hide the heaps of a famous take-away game. A move can also make a gap bigger, which that game never allows. That is why this one is sometimes called Bogus Nim.

Read the gaps as heaps

Start at the rightmost counter and count the empty squares up to the next counter. That is the first heap. Skip the next gap, count the one after it, and go on like this. With an odd number of counters, the last heap is the squares from the left edge to the leftmost counter. With counters on 3, 7 and 10, the heaps are 2 (squares 8 and 9) and 3 (squares 0 to 2); the gap between 3 and 7 is skipped. Every move changes exactly one heap.

Why it is bogus

Sliding a counter into a skipped gap makes the heap on its right bigger. In Nim a heap can only shrink. But the other player can answer at once by sliding the next counter the same distance, which puts the heap back to its old size. Such a move is called reversible: it changes nothing, and since counters only ever go left, it can be made only so many times. The game always ends.

Use the Nim-sum

Write the heap sizes in binary and combine them with XOR. The result is the Nim-sum.

Nim-sum = heap1 XOR heap2 XOR …

If it is 0, the player to move loses against perfect play. If not, some heap can be made smaller so that the Nim-sum becomes 0, and that move wins. For 2 and 3 the Nim-sum is 1, so move the counter on 3 to 2: the heaps are then 2 and 2. The Sprague–Grundy theorem explains why so many games come down to Nim in this way. We checked the rule against every position with up to 7 counters on boards of up to 16 squares, by playing each one out.

How the computer plays

The computer moves second. With a Nim-sum that is not 0 it makes the move above; otherwise it has no good move and moves at random. So you win exactly when the starting Nim-sum is not 0 and you keep handing back a 0. With Set up you can arrange a board of your own before you play.

This page differs from the original applet in small ways: you press a counter and then a square instead of dragging, the computer says which counter it moved, and the score is written out in words.

Try three counters. Work out the two heaps, then look for the one move that makes them equal.
